Street characters of Suzhou, 1516

One autumn in 1516 the Suzhou painter Zhou Chen sat at his window with nothing to do, remembered the beggars he had seen in the city's streets, and painted them, one to a leaf, twenty-four in all. Someone later mounted the album as a handscroll. Half of it is here: twelve of the figures, his own note on why he made them, and what three readers wrote after him.

1 of 17Title, written by Zhao Heqin in 1962

A handscroll is read on a table, from right to left, about an arm's length at a time: the left hand unrolls the next part while the right hand rolls up what has been seen, so the picture comes as a journey rather than all at once. Readers added to it as it passed through their hands. Huang Jishui wrote in 1564 that viewers fall about laughing at Zhou's beggars, and wished Zhou were alive to paint the men who beg for riches day and night. Zhang Fengyi thought that anyone who could look at them without pity had no kind heart. Wen Jia, in 1577, said that what each of them saw in it was their own business, and that the brushwork was beyond anyone else.

# handscroll A Chinese handscroll that you read the way one is read: right to left, an arm's length at a time. The scroll is Zhou Chen's *Beggars and Street Characters* (周臣, 流氓圖), painted in Suzhou in 1516 and now in the Cleveland Museum of Art (1964.94, CC0). Zhou painted it as an album of twenty-four figures, one to a leaf; it was later mounted as two handscrolls, and Cleveland's half holds twelve leaves, his own inscription, colophons by three later readers and a frontispiece. Those are the slides: the scroll's own sections, each a real `` cut at the scroll's own seams. A page can mount leaves of its own between them, with its own words, links and lists on them. Two ways to use it: - **A scroll scene** (`data-mode="scene"`). In the page the scroll lies closed, its brocade wrapper and Zhao Heqin's title slip up and its ribbon beside it. As you reach it and keep scrolling, it pins and opens. The closed scroll rolls to the left until its free edge comes round underneath, lays the start out to its right (the damask, the gold-flecked strip, the silk), and the stave begins to wind the start into a right-hand roll. After that, the page scroll unrolls it section by section. The page's own leaves (an About, a list of books, opening hours, a colophon with the contact address) are mounted between Zhou's openings and roll out with it. - **A carousel** (`data-mode="carousel"`, the default): it lies open, and Unroll, Back, dragging the paper, tapping a roll or the arrow keys move it a section at a time. The flat paper you look at is always the ``s, and the page's leaves are HTML. Only the rolls and the ribbon are drawn, on a WebGL2 canvas over the ends: each roll is a strip of the scroll's own paper wound on a cylinder, in the light measured on Cleveland's photograph of this scroll rolled up. For its first turn the strip is the brocade wrapper and title slip as Cleveland photographed them laid flat; after that it is the end paper. ```html

``` Links anywhere on the page to a leaf (`href="#about"`) scroll the page to where the scroll lies open at it. `demo.html` is a small press's site built this way; `carousel.html` is the carousel. ```js import { handscroll } from './handscroll.js'; const hs = handscroll(el); // also auto-starts on [data-handscroll] hs.next(); hs.prev(); hs.go(5); hs.index; // carousel: moves it; scene: scrolls the page to that section el.addEventListener('handscroll:change', (e) => e.detail); // {index, count, label} hs.destroy(); // removes the canvas, listeners and observers; back to the plain row ``` Without JS it is the row of sections, scrolling sideways and starting at the right end. Laid edge to edge, the sections are the scroll again, with the page's leaves in it. Without WebGL2 it is the same row with the buttons working. With reduced motion, a scene is the carousel: nothing pins and nothing moves by itself. ## In life, and here | In life | Here | |---|---| | A handscroll is read on a table, from right to left. The left hand unrolls about an arm's length (some 60 cm); the right hand rolls up what has been seen. The picture comes in parts, as a journey. | On a desk the window is about an arm's length of this scroll; on a phone it is one leaf and a little of the next. In the scene the page scroll does the unrolling. In the carousel Unroll does (it is on the left, because the scroll is read leftward); pull the paper to the right to unroll it, or tap a roll. ← unrolls and → rolls back. | | Closed, the scroll is wound on its roller, the start outermost. A brocade wrapper covers that outside, with the title slip pasted on it and the ribbon tied at the stave. | The closed scroll is the wrapper as Cleveland photographed it laid flat (alt13): brocade, Zhao Heqin's slip (周臣流氓圖, 1962) and the stave's folded edge, wound once round a cylinder of the measured size, slip up. The ribbon beside it is cut from Cleveland's photograph of the closed scroll (alt18), and lies where it falls in that photograph. Cleveland's rosewood weight lay on the wrapper's bottom corner; that corner is restored from the same weave one repeat away (the brocade is a regular weave), with the title slip clear of it. | | To open it, the closed scroll is rolled away from you along the table, here to the left. Its free edge comes round underneath and is laid down, and the start of the scroll lies out to the right as the roll goes on. | That, as you scroll: first the closed scroll rolls as one piece until its free edge is under it (the title slip turns away over its left side), then it lays the start out to its right. It rolls over its own ribbon, which ends up under the paper, as it would. The view keeps the scroll centred, so the free edge travels right while the roll travels left. Then the stave starts winding the start up on the right. | | The start is plain mounting: silk, a strip of gold-flecked paper, a length of damask. | The start is Cleveland's two photographs of it (alt15, alt14), from the same shoot as the full scan. They are matched to the scan and to each other by correlation (0.92 and 0.64), and each is scaled so its silk edges lie on the scan's. Where they meet the scan, one gain per channel, fitted on the white silk both show, brings them to the scan's colour. They are cut 3.4 cm short of the stave, where the weight lies on the damask in both. Cleveland's own whole-scroll stitch (alt12) puts the stave 9034 px beyond the scan; this start is 8516 px. | | Zhou Chen painted twenty-four street people in 1516, "one to a leaf", as an album. It was later mounted as two handscrolls (Cleveland and Honolulu). | The twelve figure slides are the twelve leaves, cut at their own seams in Cleveland's scan. They were mounted in pairs, so the joins between album openings are strong and the folds within them faint. Both are visible in the scan, and both were found by measurement and then checked by eye. | | A mounted scroll is a row of separate pieces: the frontispiece, the painting, the artist's own words, and the colophons later owners and friends wrote, each on its own paper between silk separators, with their seals. Albums often faced each painting with a leaf of writing (對題). | Zhao Heqin's frontispiece (1962), Zhou's inscription across the album's last opening (autumn 1516), and the colophons of Huang Jishui (1564), Zhang Fengyi and Wen Jia (1577) are sections of their own. The page's own leaves are mounted where a mounter would put them: between Zhou's openings, as facing leaves, and after the colophons, as the newest colophon. They are this scroll's own blank end paper between two strips of its own white silk, laid on the edges of the section they are joined to. Zhou's leaves stay untouched and in order. | | Rolled up, the painting faces in: what shows on the outside of each roll is the back of the mounting. Each turn is the thickness of the mounting. | Both rolls are wound face in. Each roll's outside is the back of the paper wound last (on the right) or about to come off (on the left), and it moves with the paper, so the rolls turn as it moves. The wrapper is the back of the start, so the right roll begins in brocade and the left one sheds it. The size of each roll comes from how much scroll is on it. The closed scroll is 5.05 cm across in Cleveland's photograph, which gives 5.5 px of scan per turn. The page's leaves add their own length, so with them the closed scroll is a little thicker than Cleveland's and its wrapper a little longer. | | The back of a mounted scroll is plain backing paper. | Cleveland photographed only a strip of this scroll's back, too narrow to wind. The rolls are wound in its blank end paper instead (alt11), at the scan's own scale. | | The rolls catch the light. | The light across each roll is measured on the photograph of this scroll rolled up (alt18), below the title slip and clear of the stave's fold. Cleveland lit it from the left: the left flank is brighter than the crown and the right a little darker. Nothing else is shaded. | | This scroll's roller has flush ends; its ribbon has no clasp. | So there are no knobs and no clasp: nothing is borrowed from another scroll. | | The scroll's edges are its silk borders. | The table is matted out along the scroll's own silk edge. Cleveland's scan drifts about 40 px over its length. The scan is not straightened; each roll and each page leaf is set on the paper's own edge where it touches. | ## How it is made From Cleveland's own files, all CC0: the full scan (64714 x 4862, 944 MB) and the photographs of the same scroll's wrapper (alt13), start (alt14, alt15), end paper (alt11), closed scroll (alt18) and whole mounting (alt12, for its lengths). See `assets/PICK.md` for the hunt and `assets/credits.json` for every file. - `tools/sections.py` cuts the 17 sections from the full scan. The whole scroll is resampled once to 1600 and 900 px tall and cut at whole pixels at the seams and separators, so the sections laid edge to edge are the scroll again. - `tools/start.py` makes the start from alt15 and alt14. - `tools/wrapper.py` makes the wrapper strip (with the weight's corner restored) and the silk strip. - `tools/rolls.py` makes the backing strip and the ribbon (as it lies, and turned for the carousel). It also measures the light across the roll, the paper's edges along the scroll and the scroll's build, and writes `assets/scroll.json` (keeping what the other two add). ## Runtime About 580 lines, no libraries. The track of ``s (and the page's leaves) is moved with a transform and clipped to the window between the rolls; one WebGL2 context draws the rolls and the ribbon. Each roll is a textured strip across the visible half of a cylinder. Every column of it is at the cylinder's projected x and carries the paper position that lies there and the measured light, in runs that change texture where the wrapper ends. - **Carousel stops** are worked out from the sections' own edges and the rolls' radii, so the section you go to starts exactly at the right roll. A critically damped spring takes it there. - **The scene** sets its own height (the pinned runway) from the scroll's length and maps the page scroll straight to the paper: a short hold, the roll, the laying out, then the unrolling at 1.25 page px per paper px. - **The loop** runs only while something moves, and not when the scroll is off screen. ## Options | Option | Attribute | Default | | |---|---|---|---| | `mode` | `data-mode` | `carousel` | `scene`: closed in the page, opened and unrolled by the page scroll (pinned). | | `start` | `data-start` | `0` | Carousel: the section to open at. | | | `data-title` | | Scene: what the caption says while the scroll is still rolled up. | | `src` | `data-src` | `../scroll.json` beside the images | The geometry. The textures sit beside it. | ## Theming Uses `--ink`, `--ink-2`, `--ink-3`, `--accent` (focus), `--serif`, `--sans`. | Variable | Default | | |---|---|---| | `--hs-h` | one leaf wide on a phone, up to 520 px on a desk | The scroll's height on the page. | | `--hs-max` | `520px` | The tallest it gets. | | `--hs-gap` | `clamp(14px, 3cqi, 26px)` | Between the scroll and its caption. | | `--w` (on a leaf) | | Its width in the 1600 set. | | `--paper-x` (on a page leaf) | `0%` | Which part of the end paper it is cut from (so neighbouring leaves differ). | ## Accessibility A `section` with `aria-roledescription="carousel"` and a label. The sections and page leaves are a real ordered list, each with its own label, and the figures each have a full `alt`. The buttons are real buttons, 44 px tall, disabled at the ends. - **Carousel:** the scroll itself is focusable (role `group`, labelled) and takes ←, →, Home and End. The caption is a polite live region ("3 of 17, A monkey trainer"). - **Scene:** nothing speaks while you scroll; the content is all in the page. Tabbing to a link on a page leaf, or following one, brings the page to where that leaf lies open. The canvas is `aria-hidden` and hidden in forced colours. **Reduced motion:** the carousel, with each step landing at once; dragging still moves the paper under your hand. ## Cost Sections 1.5 MB at 900 px (1x screens) or 6.4 MB at 1600 px (2x and 3x), loaded a few at a time ahead of the paper. The start is 1.3 MB at 1600 px or 0.36 MB at 900 px (damask weave does not compress), and the textures (wrapper, end paper, silk, ribbons) about 870 KB. Idle: nothing runs. Moving: one transform and one canvas draw a frame (up to six strips and a quad), DPR capped at 2. ## Credits Zhou Chen 周臣 (c. 1450–c. 1536), *Beggars and Street Characters*, 1516, handscroll, ink and light colour on paper, 31.9 x 244.5 cm. The Cleveland Museum of Art, John L. Severance Fund, 1964.94, CC0. Frontispiece and title slip by Zhao Heqin (1962); colophons by Huang Jishui (1564), Zhang Fengyi and Wen Jia (1577). Translations of the inscriptions: Cleveland's own record. The demo's press, Idle Window, is made up; its name is from Zhou's note ("閒窗", idle at my window). See `assets/credits.json`.

# handscroll: the pick

## The hunt (2026-11-03)

About 400 handscrolls looked at, and the mounting photographs that came with them:

- **Cleveland Museum of Art**, open access API, CC0: all 121 handscrolls, plus "scroll end / roller / knob / jade / ivory"
  searches (54 more). For each Chinese scroll, the stitched full-length strip and every alternate photograph that was not
  an ordinary section shot: that is where Cleveland keeps its photographs of the rolled scroll, the wrapper, the title
  slip, the ribbon and the ends. Sheets: `tools/engine/jobs/handscroll-hunt/cma/strips-1.jpg`, `strips-2.jpg`,
  `sheet-alts-1.jpg`, `sheet-alts-2.jpg`, `sheet-mounting.jpg`, `z-roll-ends.jpg`, `sheet-qianlong.jpg`,
  `sheet-1964.94-alts.jpg`.
- **The Met**, v1.1 search: 504 handscrolls listed, 179 Chinese ones read before its bot wall (Incapsula) shut this
  machine out twice; not pushed past. `tools/engine/jobs/handscroll-hunt/met/met.json`. Met wrappers seen on Commons
  (Li Jie, *Fisherman's Lodge*, DP214241: a kesi dragon wrapper with its stave and ribbon).
- **Art Institute of Chicago**: about 60 handscrolls, all served at 3000 px at most. `aic/aic.json`.
- **Wikimedia Commons** (under the shared lock): 103 + 19 files: the Palace Museum and National Palace Museum scrolls
  (Qingming Qing court version 56531x1700, *Bunian tu* 143397x9399, *Five Oxen* 63885x2560, *Spring Morning in the
  Han Palace* 52680x2683, Wang Ximeng 39974x1600, Night Revels, Admonitions, Kangxi and Qianlong tours), Met DP
  mirrors, the Walters Qiu Ying, rolled and mounted scrolls. Sheets: `commons/sheet.jpg`, `commons2/sheet.jpg`,
  `commons/sheet-got1.jpg`.
- **National Museum of Asian Art** (Freer|Sackler): the open access API was over its shared rate limit; the site's own
  search (358 Chinese handscrolls) was browsed but serves small images; no roller ends found.
- **Midjourney Explore** (read only, before the lead took Midjourney over): nothing of the real object, only CG props.
  Nothing generated; nothing needed.
- `engine.py inspect` on every downloaded candidate: jobs `handscroll-inspect-parts`, `-sec`, `-got`, `-prev`. The
  web-size previews fail on size, as they should; every print-size section and mounting photograph passes (the blank
  end papers warn "symmetric", being blank).

## Shortlist

1. **Zhou Chen 周臣, *Beggars and Street Characters* 流氓圖, 1516, Ming, Suzhou. Cleveland 1964.94, CC0.** Full scan
   64714 x 4862 (152 px per cm). Painted as an **album of 24 leaves**, one figure to a leaf, later mounted as two
   handscrolls; Cleveland has 12 leaves, Honolulu the other 12. So the sections are the painting's own: twelve leaves,
   joined in pairs (the seams between album openings are strong, the folds within them faint, both visible in the
   scan). Then Zhou Chen's own inscription (1516) across the last opening, and colophons by Huang Jishui (1564), Zhang
   Fengyi and Wen Jia (1577), each on its own paper between silk separators, and a frontispiece by Zhao Heqin (1962).
   Every part of its mounting is photographed by the museum, separately, sharp: the damask start with its stave and
   ribbon (alt14), damask, gold-flecked strip and silk (alt15), the brocade wrapper laid flat with its title slip
   "周臣流氓圖, 壬寅夏六月, 古堇趙寉亭題署" and the ribbon (alt13), the closed scroll (alt18), the blank end paper
   with a ruler (alt11). Ink and light colour on plain paper: each figure stands alone on its leaf, so it reads on a
   phone. Leaves are portrait (about 0.6), the right shape for a phone carousel.
2. Zhang Wo, *Nine Songs*, 1361, Cleveland 1959.138 (118100 x 4731). Song and picture alternate: perfect sections, and
   its rolled photographs have a title slip. But the line is so fine and the text so dense that a section at phone
   width is a pale thread.
3. *Eighteen Songs of a Nomad Flute*, early 15th c., Met 1973.120.3. Eighteen sections, colour and gold. Each section
   is a wide landscape (about 2.3 : 1): at phone width the figures are a few pixels. Met mounting photos unverified.
4. *Portraits of the Qianlong Emperor and His Twelve Consorts*, Cleveland 1969.31. Thirteen portraits, thirteen
   sections, astonishing colour; but the only stitched image is 1342 px tall, and twelve near-identical faces in a row
   make a monotonous carousel.
5. Liang Kai (attr.), *Sericulture*, Southern Song, Cleveland 1977.5. Song, a process in pictures, but three sections,
   each 3.5 : 1.
6. Ren Renfa (attr.), *Three Horses and Four Grooms*, Cleveland 1960.181. Superb, but three groups.
7. *The Lantern Night Excursion of Zhong Kui*, Cleveland 1961.206: the finest ribbon and ivory clasp photograph
   (alt0), but one continuous procession on dark silk: no sections of its own.
8. *Streams and Mountains without End*, Cleveland 1953.126; Qiu Ying's *Garden for Solitary Enjoyment*, 1978.67;
   *In the Palace*, 1976.1; and the Commons Palace Museum scrolls: continuous, so any stop would be cut where the code
   likes.

## Why this one

It is the one scroll whose sections were made as sections (album leaves), whose every mounted part was photographed
by the museum that owns it, and which holds up on a phone. Everything on the page comes from this one object:
the twelve leaves, the inscription and colophons with their seals, the frontispiece, the wrapper, the title slip and
the ribbon. One culture, one craft: Suzhou figure painting of 1516, mounted the Suzhou way.

What it lacks, said plainly: its roller has no protruding knobs (the closed scroll's ends are flush) and its ribbon has
no clasp (a museum tag is tied where a toggle would be). So there are no knobs and no clasp on the page: nothing is
borrowed from another scroll to dress it up. The back of the mounting (the outside of each roll while the scroll is
open) was not photographed; the rolls are wound in this scroll's own blank end paper (alt11), and their light is
measured from the photograph of this scroll rolled (alt18). alt12, which the lead session hoped might be the back, is the
front of the whole mounting in one stitch (stave to end paper); it gave the lengths the full scan leaves out.
